results.name: Necklace
results.description:
- Origin: Basilica of Saint Servatius, Maastricht, The Netherlands.
- Date: 6th-7th century
- Material: Amethyst, glass, copper, silver
- Capturing: Canon EOS 250D, EF-S18-135MM
- Processing: Agisoft Metashape Professional Software
- Created by: Nina Bisscheroux & Valentine Fayer

This Frankisch necklace with amethyst beads has a coin placed in the middle. This coin is Roman and displays the most recognisable symbol of Roman itself: the Lupa Capitolina or she-wolf feeding Remus and Romulus, the founders of Rome. The use of amethyst might indicate that trade was still relevant in the early Middle Ages and that Maastricht was an important city. Furthermore, the necklace consists of colored glass beads. The location of the excavation of the necklace may explain the wearers wealth, as the churchyard of the Basilica of Saint Servatius was mainly used for upper class people.

Theme: Economy and Wealth

results.name: Banjara costume
results.description:
The costume of the Banjara people, consisting of over a dozen elements, comes from the village of Hampi in India, in the state of Karnataka. It was brought to Poland and resold to the District Museum in Tarnów in 2001 by an ethnology student (supervised by Prof. Lech Mróz, PhD habilitated) of the University of Warsaw, who conducted field research among nomadic peoples in India. The costume is displayed on a mannequin as part of the permanent exhibition Romani People: History and Culture, which has been presented at the Ethnographic Museum in Tarnów since 1990.

results.name: Coatlicue
results.description:
Coatlicue is represented as a woman wearing a skirt of writhing snakes and a necklace made of human hearts, hands, and skulls. Her feet and hands are adorned with claws and her breasts are depicted as hanging flaccid from pregnancy. Her face is formed by two facing serpents (after her head was cut off and the blood spurt forth from her neck in the form of two gigantic serpents), referring to the myth that she was sacrificed during the beginning of the present creation.

Mask made by Isaias Morales in cartonería: The Mexican art of papier mache, displayed at Världskulturmuseét, Gothenburg, Sweden.

results.name: Malachite
results.description:
I found this mineral in my mom's display cabinet. She has no idea where it came from. Could it be malachite?

Malachite is a copper carbonate with distinctive green veining. Though not a particularly hard stone, it takes an excellent polish. Malachite is usually found near copper ore deposits. The most famous malachite mines were in the Ural mountains in Russia, where 20 ton blocks were once taken from the quarries to decorate the palaces of the Russian tsars. Today malachite is a scarcer material and the most important producer is the Congo (formerly known as Zaire).
Malachite is indeed one of the most popular green gems and is frequently used in gemstone rings, - it is very-well suited for other types of gemstone jewelry, including gemstone earrings, pins and brooches, as well as in necklaces and fine gemstone pendants.

results.name: Incense Burner
results.description:
Miniature Teotihuacan-style incense. The lid depicts a figure wearing a tall headdress with zoomorphic design, with open eyes and mouth, followed by a band with four floral motifs. The face is painted red and displays open eyes, an aquiline nose with a nose ornament, earflares, and a necklace with circular beads. The figure features extended arms, holding two rectangular shields; at the center of the torso there is a horizontal band with a circular appliqué in yellow and red. The bowl has a convex base, a pedestal support, and rectangular handles on the sides. The decoration includes a central talud design, with a red horizontal band at the upper section and another at the lower section, as well as circular appliqués in the middle zone of the bowl. 

 IDAEH Cultural Property No. 1.2.144.1251
 
www.fundacionrutamaya.org

Special thanks to the staff of La Ruta Maya Foundation for their hard work on this project.

3D model made in RealityScan; Total # of images: 293
